newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire offers flexibility on refugee aid.
newsitem.headline: Zaire offers flexibility on refugee aid.

text.p: Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said on Wednesday his country was prepared to be "flexible" to ensure that emergency food aid reached civilians and refugees fleeing a Tutsi revolt in the east.

Kengo, speaking after talks with U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien, said Zaire accepted the idea of a multinational force under Canadian command but stressed that protected aid corridors should be designed to ensure a return home of all refugees.
"In order to bring food supplies to the displaced and refugees, Zaire must be prepared to be flexible if necessary," Kengo told reporters.
Hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi and displaced Zairean civilians have fled fighting in Zaire's eastern refugee provinces of North and South Kivu.
Many fled to Zaire in 1994 fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis in neighbouring Rwanda.
Chretien paid tribute to Kengo's commitment, which followed earlier Zairean statements that any shipment of aid through rebel-held territory would violate its sovereignty.
"It's extremely important that the Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo has expressed his willingness not to use international principles as a barrier to aiding the refugees very, very quickly," he said.
"Zaire is prepared to show some flexibility but they are very, very concerned that these shipments cannot be used for any other purpose except bringing essential humanitarian aid in," he added.
Chretien said Zaire placed responsibility for ensuring the humanitarian nature of the aid with the United Nations.
Aid efforts in the east, where Tutsi rebels control a string of towns, have been complicated by Zairean accusations of territorial violations by Tutsi-led Rwanda, a charge Rwanda denies.

The U.N. and other relief agencies transported supplies into the eastern town of Goma on Monday after negotiations with the rebels, who launched an offensive on October 18 near the border with Burundi, accusing Kinshasa of denying them citizenship.
Kengo said Zaire had given its agreement to the proposed force, designed to ensure security for relief workers and the refugees, but he added:
"We wish that the relief corridor will be designed in such a way for the refugees to go back to their homeland and so that no more camps will be established in North and South Kivu."

With the notable exception of the giant Mugunga camp, the world's largest, refugees have deserted camps in the region. Refugees say armed Hutu hardliners blamed for the 1994 massacres had taken refuge in Mugunga.
